0.title: Growing Up with Jesus
0.essay:
This study is for you if you are about nine to twelve years old. These are big years. Your body is changing, your friendships are changing, and you are starting to ask your own questions about God. That is a good thing.

Your questions matter

Maybe you have wondered: Is God really there? Does he love me even when I mess up? Why do my friends leave me out? Is it wrong to want a phone like everyone else? God is not cross with you for asking. The Bible is full of people who asked God hard questions, and he answered them.

Jesus loved children. When grown-ups tried to send them away, he said, “Let the children come to me; do not hinder them, for to such belongs the kingdom of God” (Mark 10:14). He has time for you.

The chapters

1. Who Am I?: made and loved by God, as your body changes. 2. Is It True?: questions about God, the Bible and becoming a Christian. 3. Friends, Family and Fitting In. 4. Screens, Games and What I Watch. 5. Brave and Kind at School.

A note for parents

Read these chapters with your child, a chapter a week, and talk about the questions at the end. Children of this age are often more open than they will be in a few years’ time. Now is the time to build trust, so that they will keep coming to you when the questions get harder.

For reflection

What is one question about God you have wanted to ask? Write it down, and ask a parent or a Christian you trust this week.

1.title: Who Am I?
1.essay:
Lots of voices tell you who you are: your friends, your marks at school, how you look, how good you are at sport. God has the first and last word. You are someone he made on purpose and loves.

Made by God

The Bible says God made people “in his own image” (Genesis 1:27). That means you are like a picture of God. You can think, love, make things, laugh and pray. No animal can do that. You were not an accident. David prayed, “For you formed my inward parts; you knitted me together in my mother’s womb” (Psalm 139:13). God planned your eyes, your voice and the way you are.

A changing body

Around this age, your body starts to change. You grow taller, your voice or shape changes, and you may feel things you have not felt before. This is called puberty, and it is part of God’s good design to turn you slowly from a child into an adult. It can feel strange or embarrassing. You are not weird. Talk to your mum or dad, or another adult you trust, about anything that worries you.

Comparing

It is easy to compare yourself with others. She is prettier. He is better at football. They have more stuff. Comparing usually makes us either proud or sad. But God did not make you to be someone else. Paul says that in God’s family, everyone is different, like the parts of a body, and every part is needed (1 Corinthians 12:18–20).

Loved when you mess up

Everyone does wrong things. The Bible calls it sin. You know that feeling when you have lied or been unkind. But God does not stop loving his children when they sin. He sent Jesus to take the punishment for our sin, so that we can be forgiven. “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins” (1 John 1:9).

A real-life moment

Sam wasn’t picked for the school team, and his best friend was. On the way home he felt like a nobody. That night his dad reminded him that God doesn’t choose his children by how good they are at sport. Sam still felt disappointed. But he went to sleep knowing he was loved.

For reflection

What is one thing you sometimes wish were different about yourself? Thank God that he made you and loves you, just as you are, and that he is still at work in you.

2.title: Is It True?
2.essay:
As you grow, you may start to wonder whether the things you have heard about God are really true, or just what your parents believe. That is a good question to ask. Christianity is not afraid of questions.

Is God real?

Look around: the stars, the ocean, your own beating heart. All of it points to a maker. “The heavens declare the glory of God, and the sky above proclaims his handiwork” (Psalm 19:1). But God has done more than make the world. He has spoken to us in the Bible, and he came to us in Jesus.

Is the Bible true?

The Bible was written over many hundreds of years by many people, yet it tells one story, about God rescuing his people through Jesus. Its writers often told the truth even when it made them look bad. And many people saw Jesus alive after he died. Paul says that more than five hundred people saw him at one time, and most of them were still alive when he wrote (1 Corinthians 15:6). People could check!

Am I a Christian?

Some children grow up always loving Jesus. Others come to faith later. A Christian is not someone who goes to church or has Christian parents. It is someone who trusts Jesus. You know you have done wrong; you believe Jesus died for you and rose again; and you want to follow him. “If you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved” (Romans 10:9).

You don’t need to know exactly when you started believing. What matters is whether you trust Jesus now. If you are not sure, pray and tell him, and talk to your parents or a church leader.

When you have doubts

Having questions does not mean you are not a Christian. A father once said to Jesus, “I believe; help my unbelief!” (Mark 9:24). Jesus helped him. Bring your doubts to God and to a Christian you trust. It is better to ask than to hide them.

A real-life moment

Mia’s friend said, “Science proves God isn’t real.” Mia didn’t know what to say. At home she asked her mum, who showed her that many great scientists have been Christians, and that science shows us how God’s world works. Mia went back the next day with a better answer and a smile.

For reflection

Do you trust Jesus for yourself? If you are not sure, who could you talk to about it this week?

3.title: Friends, Family and Fitting In
3.essay:
Friends become very important at this age. So does fitting in. God cares about your friendships and your family, and he can help you to be a good friend, even when it is hard.

Wanting to fit in

Everybody wants to belong. Sometimes that means pressure to wear the right clothes, laugh at mean jokes, or leave someone else out. The Bible warns, “Bad company ruins good morals” (1 Corinthians 15:33). The people you spend time with shape who you become. Choose friends who are kind and honest, and be that kind of friend.

When you are left out

Being left out hurts. If it happens to you, remember that Jesus was rejected too, even by his closest friends. He knows how it feels. Tell God and tell a grown-up. And remember the feeling, so that you notice when someone else is on their own. Go and sit with them.

Being a good friend

“A friend loves at all times” (Proverbs 17:17). A good friend tells the truth, keeps secrets that should be kept (but not secrets about someone being hurt), says sorry, and forgives. Jesus said, “whatever you wish that others would do to you, do also to them” (Matthew 7:12).

Your parents

“Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right” (Ephesians 6:1). As you grow, you may start to disagree with your parents more. That is normal. But God gave them to you to love and guide you. Obeying them is a way of trusting God. When you disagree, tell them respectfully, rather than sulking or shouting. And if a grown-up ever asks you to do something wrong or unsafe, you do not have to obey; tell another adult you trust.

Brothers and sisters

Siblings can be the hardest people to love, because you see them every day. But home is where you practise being like Jesus. Share, say sorry, and stick up for each other.

A real-life moment

Ella’s group decided to stop talking to a girl called Grace. Ella felt sick about it, but she was afraid of being left out herself. In the end, she sat with Grace at lunch. Two of the others joined them the next day.

For reflection

Is there someone at school or church who is often on their own? What could you do this week to include them?

4.title: Screens, Games and What I Watch
4.essay:
Phones, tablets, games and videos can be fun and useful. They can also take over your time and put things into your mind that are not good for you. God wants to help you use them wisely.

Good gifts, used well

Technology is not evil. You can use it to learn, to make things, to talk to grandparents and to enjoy good stories. But like sweets, too much is bad for you, and some kinds are poison.

Guarding your mind

What you watch and listen to shapes your heart. Paul says, “whatever is true, whatever is honorable, whatever is just, whatever is pure, whatever is lovely, whatever is commendable, if there is any excellence, if there is anything worthy of praise, think about these things” (Philippians 4:8). Ask: Is this true? Is it kind? Is it pure? Would I be happy watching it with Jesus sitting next to me? Because he is.

If you see something bad

Sometimes, even without looking for it, you may see pictures or videos of people without clothes, or of violence, that make you feel shocked or confused. If that happens, it is not your fault. Turn it off, and tell your parents or another adult you trust. You will not be in trouble for telling. Keeping it secret only makes it grow.

Staying safe online

Never share your address, school or photos with people you do not know in real life. If anyone online asks you to keep a secret from your parents, or to send pictures, stop and tell an adult straight away. That is a warning sign of someone who wants to hurt you.

Time

Games and videos are designed to keep you playing and watching. Hours can disappear. “Look carefully then how you walk, not as unwise but as wise, making the best use of the time” (Ephesians 5:15–16). Agree on screen limits with your parents, and keep screens out of your bedroom at night. Go outside, read, make things, and spend time with people face to face.

A real-life moment

Josh was playing an online game when a stranger started asking him personal questions and said, “Don’t tell your parents.” Josh remembered what his dad had said and told him. His dad thanked him for being brave, and reported the account.

For reflection

Is there something you watch or play that you would not want Jesus to see? What could you change this week?

5.title: Brave and Kind at School
5.essay:
School is where you spend much of your week. It is a place to learn, to make friends and to live for Jesus. Sometimes it is also a place of worry, unkindness or pressure. God goes with you through the school gate.

When you are worried

Tests, new classes, friendship problems: lots of things can make you anxious. Jesus says, “do not be anxious about tomorrow” (Matthew 6:34). That doesn’t mean pretending not to feel worried. It means taking your worries to God. The Bible tells you to keep on “casting all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you” (1 Peter 5:7). Tell him exactly what is worrying you, and tell a grown-up too.

Bullying

If someone is hurting you, calling you names or spreading lies about you, tell a teacher and your parents. That is not telling tales. It is asking for help, and God puts adults in your life to protect you. If you see someone else being bullied, do not join in or laugh. Stand with them, and tell an adult. “Open your mouth for the mute, for the rights of all who are destitute” (Proverbs 31:8).

Doing your best

Schoolwork can be boring or hard. But you can do it for God. “Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men” (Colossians 3:23). That means trying your best, not cheating, and being honest when you haven’t done your homework. Your worth is not your marks, but your effort can honour God.

Standing up for Jesus

Sometimes other children may laugh at you for being a Christian. Daniel was a teenager when he was taken to Babylon, and he decided not to do what was wrong, even though it was risky (Daniel 1:8). You can be brave too, in small ways: praying before lunch, saying you go to church, refusing to join in with something wrong. You don’t need to preach at people. Be kind, be honest, and be ready to say why you love Jesus.

Kind to everyone

Be kind to the new child, the one who is different, the teacher having a bad day. “Be kind to one another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you” (Ephesians 4:32). Kindness is one of the clearest ways to show what Jesus is like.

A real-life moment

In assembly, a boy in Noah’s class made fun of people who pray. Noah’s face went red. Later, the boy asked him quietly, “Do you actually pray?” Noah said yes, and that he’d prayed for his grandma when she was ill. The boy said his own grandma was ill. They talked for the whole of break.

For reflection

What is one way you could be brave for Jesus, or kind to someone, at school this week?
